title: Distributed Semantics for Distributed Quantum Computing
abstract: We present a quantum process calculus that can split the system state along process boundaries and follow the evolution of each process in isolation, without losing information about the joint state-a property we call spatial compositionality. Compositionality is the key to reasoning about any complex system, yet quantum process calculi have struggled to provide its spatial kind, which would enable analyzing a system one process at a time. Many a quantum process calculi have been proposed, but they invariably rely on a global state representation based on state vectors or density matrices, with no known way to split them without losing information about entanglement. We propose to model quantum states with Deutsch-Hayden descriptors instead, which provide a modular representation of qubit states and their evolution. We adapt these descriptors to allow arbitrary splitting and merging of the store of qubits, leading to an unusual process calculus in which qubit transfer messages carry the actual state of the qubit, where existing calculi transfer only a reference. The calculus gives localized views of system state visible to each process, which can be assembled back together into the joint state. We define a notion of process equivalence with extensive justification grounded in physics and show a bisimulation whose soundness proof is simplified by spatial compositionality. The calculus can model open systems entangled with external processes, and we demonstrate this capability on a fragment of the BB84 key distribution protocol. This exercise shows that Deutsch-Hayden descriptors can successfully track qubit movements across process and system boundaries, though it needs help from density matrices to reason about information flow.
summary: The paper introduces DH-CCS, a novel quantum process calculus that represents quantum states using Deutsch-Hayden descriptors instead of global state vectors. This descriptor approach grants 'spatial compositionality,' enabling the rigorous analysis of complex, distributed quantum systems by allowing processes to evolve independently while correctly accounting for entanglement across boundaries.
main_problem: The core problem is developing a quantum process calculus that achieves 'spatial compositionality'—the ability to analyze complex, entangled systems by treating individual processes in isolation without losing joint state information.
main_result: The authors propose using Deutsch-Hayden (DH) descriptors within a new quantum process calculus (DH-CCS), which successfully models qubit movement across process boundaries while preserving entanglement structure.
method: They adapt DH descriptors to provide a modular, name-based representation of quantum states, allowing for arbitrary splitting and merging that overcomes the limitations of global state vector representations.
model_or_system: The model is an abstract quantum process calculus (DH-CCS) designed to reason about distributed quantum computation. It models qubits using DH descriptors ($\mathfrak{q}$), which are sets of Pauli operators acting on named variables, allowing for local tracking of state evolution.
key_observables: The primary diagnostic tool is the set of DH descriptors $\mathfrak{q}$, which track the evolution of observables like Pauli $X$ and $Z$ operators for each qubit. Security analysis tracks correlations between qubits (e.g., in BB84).
important_parameters: The structure relies on stable, name-based identifiers for qubits rather than position-dependent indices.
main_assumptions: DH descriptors are excellent for tracking physical movement across boundaries but require density matrices to accurately account for information flow and entanglement collapse. The calculus also leaves out classical control derived from measurement results.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the syntax of DH-CCS, detailing production rules for actions like splitting ($c!x.P$), conditional operations, and parallel composition ($\|$) that enforce compositional semantics.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first identifying the need for spatial compositionality, proposing DH descriptors as a solution to monolithic state limitations, developing the calculus (DH-CCS) with name-based indexing, demonstrating its utility in modeling open systems (BB84), and finally discussing equivalence notions and remaining theoretical gaps.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly formal, compositional framework for analyzing quantum protocols. For AMO/open systems researchers, it offers an algebraic tool to reason about local interactions and entanglement flow without relying solely on computationally intractable global density matrix evolution.
